**Work in progress, 31 October 2026.** The VPP runs end to end, but the sails are not simulated yet
and nothing has been checked against a real boat. Read its race times as comparisons between
designs, not as predictions.

## What the VPP does {#sec-what}

The other studies on this site compare fins, sections and bulbs by the forces the simulations give.
A velocity prediction program (VPP) turns those forces into boat speed. For each wind speed and
angle it finds the steady state in which the forces balance [@parolini2007]:

* the sails' drive equals the drag of the hull and appendages;
* the sails' side force equals the side force the keel, hull and rudder make at some leeway;
* the sails' heeling moment equals the righting moment;
* the rudder holds the boat on course.

It solves for boat speed, heel, leeway and rudder angle, and flattens the sails as far as that pays.
The result is a polar (@fig-vpp-polar). From the best course upwind and downwind it then times a
windward-leeward race, averaged over the winds a club races in.

![The polar of an example run: boat speed against the true wind angle, one curve per wind speed. The
red points are the best VMG (velocity made good) upwind and downwind, which the race
uses.](../_generated/vpp-polar.svg){#fig-vpp-polar}

Each run writes one self-contained page: the polar, every part's forces at every point, the balance
at any point, the hydrostatics and mass budget, the race (with wind weights you can change) and
how race time responds to small changes. [An example run's report](../runs/vpp/iom-alternative/20261031-162130/report.html)
is published here as it was written.

The example uses the "Alternative" IOM hull, because I have its lines as an STL file. The file is
private and can't be distributed without a licence; the numbers derived from it can. The fin and bulb
are the ones the [fin section](../custom-section/) and [bulb](../bulb-design/) studies arrived at,
with the A rig.

## Where it stands {#sec-progress}

**Working:**

* **The solver.** All four balances, including the yaw balance with the rudder, with the sails'
  flattening and sail set chosen for speed. With the same forces it gives the same speeds as
  Python-VPP [@pyvpp].
* **Any hull from its lines.** Sinkage, trim and righting moment of an STL hull at any heel, under
  the other parts' forces.
* **CFD in the boat model.** The keel (fin, bulb and hull together, over heel, leeway and speed), the
  hull's form factor and the windage of the topsides come from simulations of the hull in use.
* **The race and the report.** Best VMG, race time over a club's winds, exchange rates (the race
  time per small change in a part), and the page above.

**Not yet:** the sails, which are next; the hull's waves; laminar flow; and a check against a real
boat (@sec-trust).

## Where each force comes from {#sec-sources}

| part | what it supplies | model | from CFD? |
|:-------|:-----------------|:---------------------|:--------|
| sails | all the drive, the heeling force and moment | the ORC's coefficients for full-size main and jib [@orc-vpp2026] | **no** |
| keel (fin and bulb) | most of the side force; about a third of the drag upwind | a table of 3D simulations of fin, bulb and hull over heel, leeway and speed | yes |
| hull, friction | about a quarter of the drag upwind | the ITTC-57 friction line times a form factor from CFD | the form factor |
| hull, waves | a sixth to almost half of the drag upwind, rising with the wind; about half downwind in a breeze | Michell's thin-ship theory [@michell1898] | **no** |
| rudder | the yaw balance; a tenth to a sixth of the drag upwind | lifting-line theory in the keel's downwash | **no** |
| windage | side force, lift and a little drag from the topsides | a table of CFD of the hull above the water | yes, without the rig |
| righting moment | the moment that keeps the boat upright | the hull's lines floated at heel with the mass budget | geometry, not CFD |

: Where each part's forces come from. {#tbl-vpp-sources}

All of the drag is balanced by the sails' drive, and the sails are not simulated. Of the drag
itself, the models built on CFD cover most in light air; as the wind rises, the hull's waves, from
theory, grow to about half (@fig-vpp-drag).

![Each part's drag at the best-VMG points of the example run, coloured by where its model comes
from: greens are built on CFD, hatched earth tones on theory. The height of each bar is the drag the
sails' drive balances.](../_generated/vpp-drag.svg){#fig-vpp-drag}

## How far to trust it {#sec-trust}

The shortcomings, the largest first. The confidence ratings are my judgement from the findings logs.

| | what it covers | confidence | the main unknown |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| sails (@sec-sails) | all the drive | low | coefficients for full-size yachts, not IOM sails |
| calibration (@sec-calibration) | everything | none | no measured IOM speeds |
| hull waves (@sec-waves) | up to half the drag | low to medium | thin-ship theory, no free-surface CFD |
| laminar flow (@sec-laminar) | the friction of every part | medium | all the CFD is fully turbulent |
| keel and hull form factor (@sec-keel) | side force, viscous drag | medium to high | a double body, the mesh |
| rudder (@sec-rudder) | yaw balance | medium; low at large angles | no stall, no CFD |
| windage (@sec-windage) | side force and lift of the topsides | medium | no sails over the deck |
| steady sailing (@sec-steady) | the race | for comparisons only | flat water, steady wind |
| assumed inputs (@sec-inputs) | masses, winds, course | medium | estimated masses, assumed winds |

: The confidence in each part, in short. {#tbl-vpp-trust}

### The sails are not simulated: the next focus {#sec-sails}

This is the largest gap. The sails make all the drive and all the heeling force, so an error in them
goes straight into the boat speed, heel and leeway, and through those into every other part's forces.

* **The coefficients are for full-size yachts.** The ORC's coefficients [@orc-vpp2026] were fitted at
  Reynolds numbers 10–100 times an IOM's. On an IOM's sails the flow can stay laminar and separate in
  ways it doesn't at full size. How far off they are is not known.
* **One way to depower.** The model only flattens the sails, and in a breeze it runs out. Twist,
  sheeting and mast bend are not in it, and only the A rig is modelled.
* **Downwind,** the goose-winged jib has no coefficients of its own.
* **One wind for the whole rig:** the change of wind up the mast is ignored.

**The sails are the next focus.** The project has a sail simulation, which runs but is not yet
validated. The plan is to simulate the A rig and put its forces into the VPP in place of ORC's.

### Nothing has been checked against a real boat {#sec-calibration}

No measured speed, heel or leeway of a real IOM has been compared with the VPP's. Unit tests and the
Python-VPP cross-check show the solver does its arithmetic right, not that the forces describe a real
boat. The only other IOM VPP found, Lester Gilbert's spreadsheet, is not calibrated either
[@gilbert-simplevpp]. GPS logs of an IOM in measured wind would be the first check.

### The hull's waves come from theory {#sec-waves}

The hull simulations have no free surface: the hull is mirrored at the waterline, which gives
friction and form drag but no waves. The waves come from Michell's thin-ship theory, which is known
to exaggerate the humps and hollows of wave resistance at the speeds an IOM sails upwind, has no
heel, and is out of its depth with the bow trimmed down in a breeze.

### Laminar flow is left out {#sec-laminar}

Every simulation behind the VPP treats the flow as turbulent from the leading edge. At an IOM's
Reynolds numbers much of it is laminar, with less friction. So the absolute drag is probably too
high, and a design's laminar-flow advantage, such as the HT35 fin's ([fin section
page](../custom-section/)), is not in the keel table.

### The keel and the hull's form factor {#sec-keel}

The parts most firmly based on CFD: 3D simulations of fin, bulb and hull over heel, leeway and speed.
They are double bodies, so no waves; the leeway drag depends on the mesh; the fin's stall is unsteady
flow solved as steady; and the table holds each heel's static trim, not the bow-down trim downwind.
The form factor rests on a few simulations that resolve the wall.

### The rudder: no stall, no CFD {#sec-rudder}

A lifting line in the keel's estimated downwash, with no stall model. Fine at small angles; in strong
wind the VPP asks for rudder angles a real rudder would stall at, so those points are optimistic.

### Windage without the rig {#sec-windage}

The topsides' forces come from CFD of the hull above the water, without sails, in a uniform wind.
Upwind the jib and main turn the wind over the deck, which the table doesn't see. The direction of
the effect (side force and lift, little drag) is likely right; its size less so.

### Steady sailing in flat water {#sec-steady}

The VPP describes a boat sailing straight at a steady speed: no waves, gusts or shifts, a fixed time
per tack and gybe, no starts or other boats, and perfect trim. Its race time measures boat speed, not
race results.

### Assumed inputs {#sec-inputs}

The masses other than the bulb, fin and rig are estimates; the hull's waterline is assumed; the
club's winds are an assumed distribution, not measured; the course is two laps of 100 m legs.

## What it is good for, and what's next {#sec-use}

**Good for:**

* comparing designs that differ in a part the CFD models (two keels, fins or bulbs on the same hull),
  sailed with the same sails, as a ranking under the model rather than a measured gain;
* seeing how large each force is on each point of sail and in each wind (@fig-vpp-drag);
* trade-offs through the exchange rates, such as righting moment against drag.

**Not for:** absolute boat speeds, anything that depends on the sails' shape or trim, strong winds,
or predicting race results.

**Next,** roughly in order:

1. the sails: simulate the A rig and replace the ORC coefficients;
2. a real-boat check: GPS speed and heel of an IOM in measured wind;
3. free-surface simulations of the hull at a few points, against the thin-ship waves;
4. laminar flow on the keel;
5. a rudder stall model, and the smaller rigs for strong winds;
6. windage with the rig over the deck.
